title: Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
objective: Evaluate readiness across people, processes, data, technology, and governance, and safely scale AI from pilots to an organization-wide level.

prerequisites.title: AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

sections.title: Do not confuse pilot success with enterprise-wide scaling
paragraphs: A pilot is the stage at which hypotheses and value are tested with specific users, limited data, and a clearly defined business challenge. Do not decide to scale company-wide based on a single successful example. Identify the conditions under which the impact can be reproduced, the conditions that led to failure, and the data, business processes, and capabilities required.

Scaling across the enterprise requires establishing objectives for each user department, common data definitions, access management, training, support, change management, and operational accountability. Even when the approach is extended to other departments, the same KPIs and workflows may not be applicable.

Before expanding the scope of use, test the solution on a small scale in the next department and measure both its effectiveness and the burden on the people using it. Even if accuracy meets the required standard, limit the scope of use and establish procedures and controls when there is no person responsible for handling exceptions or when the solution is being used outside its approved purposes.

sections.title: Measure Readiness Across People and Processes, Not Just Technology
paragraphs: When evaluating AI readiness, do not look only at whether the available tools exist. For people, assess decision-maker support, user literacy, collaboration with specialists, and the ability to adapt to changing roles. For processes, assess current workflows, decision points where AI outputs are used, exception handling, and the handoff of responsibility.

For data and technology readiness, assess data ownership, quality, access, update frequency, integration methods, and security. Having “a lot of data” does not mean that the data is fit for purpose, can be used safely, and has explainable quality.
A maturity assessment is not complete when departments have merely been ranked. Use it to make gaps visible and to progressively build the capabilities needed, starting with high-value use cases.

sections.title: Adoption Is an Initiative That Changes Users’ Roles and Capabilities
paragraphs: When introducing AI, clarify what frontline teams will automate, what they will verify, and which decisions people will continue to make. An abstract explanation that “AI will replace people” alone does not enable users to understand the purpose, their responsibilities, or the capabilities they need, nor does it establish safe use.

Leaders involve business users, technical teams, and risk, legal, and security functions from an early stage, and incorporate user feedback into improvements. Training covers not only tool operation but also the limitations of outputs, verification methods, handling of confidential information, and reporting abnormal situations.

Adoption outcomes are not measured solely by usage volume. They are evaluated based on working time, quality, customer impact, employee workload, exception handling, and changes in risk; leaders also decide whether to scale back or stop use that does not serve its purpose.

sources.label: Responsible AI: From Principles to Practice

checkpoints.prompt: A retail company’s AI leader has successfully piloted an inventory replenishment AI at one store. Before deciding whether to expand it to other stores, which approach is most appropriate for determining whether it can deliver value safely while accounting for differences between stores?

choices.text: Roll it out to all stores at the same time based solely on the success at one store.
choices.explanation: This expands the impact of failures without checking differences in data, operations, training, controls, or user acceptance across stores.

choices.text: At each stage, check the evidence of value, readiness, controls, and user acceptance, then expand while refining the design based on what is learned.
choices.explanation: Add stores incrementally and verify the effects on stockouts and waste. Also confirm that each store has the necessary data, that staff can handle exceptions, and that the defined scope of use is being followed. If issues arise, review the procedures and controls, and expand to the next store only after the conditions are met.

choices.text: Eliminate store-specific exception handling and require staff to follow the AI’s recommendations.
choices.explanation: This removes operational accountability and frontline judgment, preventing a safe response to incorrect recommendations.

choices.text: Use usage count as the only KPI and do not measure the impact on stockouts or waste.
choices.explanation: Usage count alone cannot evaluate business value or undesirable impacts.

checkpoints.prompt: A manufacturing company executive is assessing readiness to deploy maintenance AI across multiple factories. Each factory already has AI tools in place, but the owners and quality standards for equipment data differ by factory, and on-site exception procedures have not been documented. What is the most appropriate next action?

choices.text: Because the tools are available, apply the same settings to every factory without checking differences in data and business procedures.
choices.explanation: The mere presence of technology does not demonstrate readiness in terms of data quality, accountability, exception handling, or on-site use.

choices.text: Rank the factories by maturity and permanently prohibit AI use at the lower-ranked factories.
choices.explanation: The purpose of a maturity assessment is to identify capability gaps and create a phased improvement plan.

choices.text: Decide on the deployment plan using only the technical team, without involving on-site personnel.
choices.explanation: This can overlook issues involving actual operational decisions, exceptions, acceptance, and training, making successful adoption less likely.

choices.text: Assess data ownership, quality, access, exception procedures, and user capabilities, then create a plan for standardization and factory-specific improvements.
choices.explanation: Correct. Assess people, processes, data, technology, and governance together to establish the prerequisites for safe deployment across factories.

checkpoints.prompt: A department head at an insurance company is introducing an AI tool that summarizes contracts. Frontline staff are concerned that the operating model may involve sending the AI output directly to customers. From the perspectives of user capability and change management, which response is most appropriate?

choices.text: Prioritize speed of implementation and provide no training on verifying or reporting outputs or handling exceptions.
choices.explanation: Users will not understand the system's limitations or how to respond to abnormal situations, so inaccurate outputs could directly affect customers.

choices.text: Treat the AI's output as always correct and prohibit staff from exercising their judgment.
choices.explanation: This eliminates the need for human review and responsible use, leaving staff unable to respond to exceptions or errors.

choices.text: Incorporate the AI's role, the points staff must verify, exception reporting, handling of confidential information, and success metrics into work procedures and training.
choices.explanation: Correct. Users can understand the AI's limitations and their own responsibilities, helping embed the change safely and measurably.

choices.text: Train users only on how to operate the tool and make no changes to work assignments or success metrics.
choices.explanation: Operational training alone does not clarify who verifies the output, under what conditions work is handed off to a person, or what counts as a successful outcome.
